analysis.one_liner: Gives renters a refundable federal tax credit for rent that exceeds 30% of their income.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote, one of roughly 11,000 House bills introduced in the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Rent Relief Act would have created a refundable tax credit for renters who pay more than 30% of their income in rent — the government's standard line for "rent-burdened." Households earning $25,000 or less would have gotten back 100% of the rent above that 30% line, with the share sliding to 25% for incomes between $75,000 and $100,000, and nothing for anyone over $100,000. It also directed the Treasury to pay the credit out monthly during the year, so people wouldn't have to wait for tax season.
analysis.who_benefits: Rent-burdened tenants, especially low- and moderate-income renters. A renter making $20,000 and paying $9,000 a year in rent would have received a credit for 100% of the amount above $6,000 (30% of income) — here, $3,000 — capped at what HUD considers fair market rent for their area. Because the credit is refundable, people who owe little or no federal income tax would still get the money. The monthly advance-payment option would have put relief in renters' hands throughout the year rather than as a tax-season lump sum.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit covering 25% to 100% of the rent a household pays above 30% of its adjusted gross income, with the full 100% for incomes up to $25,000, 75% up to $50,000, 50% up to $75,000, and 25% up to $100,000.
The credit is refundable and counts utilities, so it reaches renters who owe little or no income tax and captures their full housing cost.
Treasury would have to set up a program to pay the credit monthly in advance, so relief arrives when the rent is due rather than at tax time.
Rent above 100% of HUD's small-area fair market rent doesn't count toward the credit, which limits how much the benefit could inflate rents in overpriced buildings.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill contains no revenue offset, so the new credit would have been deficit-financed. Landlords benefit indirectly, since money that eases renters' cost burden flows into the rental market — though the fair-market-rent cap keeps the credit from paying rents HUD already deems above market.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no pay-for: it adds a new entitlement to the deficit without raising revenue anywhere else, and a broad rent credit is one of the more expensive benefits Congress could design.

The credit is measured against adjusted gross income, so a household with low reported income — retirees, self-employed people with write-offs — could qualify even with substantial assets, while the relief does nothing about the underlying shortage of affordable housing.
Because the credit counts only rent up to HUD's small-area fair market rent, tenants in units priced above that benchmark get no help with the most expensive part of their rent.
A good-faith objection: subsidizing rental demand without adding supply can push rents up, so some of the credit's value could end up in landlords' pockets rather than renters'.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and well-targeted: it goes to people spending an unaffordable share of income on rent, phases out at $100,000, and arrives monthly. The honest cost is that it is entirely deficit-financed and doesn't address housing supply, so part of the subsidy could be captured by landlords through higher rents. The fair-market-rent cap blunts but doesn't eliminate that risk. On balance it is a serious, if costly, attempt at the largest recurring expense most low-income households face.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Danny K. Davis of Illinois introduced the bill on July 13, 2022, with Reps. Gomez, Peters, and Panetta joining as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No hearing, markup, or floor action followed; the bill's action history ends with the committee referral, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Renters got nothing, and the federal Treasury kept the money it would have spent. The credit design — with its income phase-down and fair-market-rent cap — left the ledger with no change at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and the status quo; renters got nothing

for.name: Rep. Danny K. Davis
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Rent Relief Act of 2022 and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: Reps. Jimmy Gomez, Scott Peters, and Jimmy Panetta
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill drew 5 Democratic cosponsors in total and no Republicans.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Richard Neal, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and with no recorded votes the bill's partisan shape rests on sponsorship alone: 6 Democrats, 0 Republicans.

industries.note: A refundable rent credit funnels public money to renters, who spend it on rent; landlords benefit indirectly from tenants better able to pay. The bill caps the credit at HUD's fair market rent, which limits how much landlords above that line could capture, and opponents note that boosting rental demand without new supply can push rents up.
The bill creates a large new refundable credit with no revenue offset, so the cost falls on the deficit and future taxpayers. It died before any spending occurred.
